blocks.text: 1. Sentence Chunking
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446842034-278438975.png

Sliding Window Chunking splits text using a fixed size window that slides forward with overlap. Sentence Chunking pushes structural awareness to its finest level, splitting strictly along sentence boundaries.
It treats each individual sentence, or a small group of them, as its own chunk.
2. The Sentence As A Natural Unit
A sentence already expresses one complete, self contained idea.
That makes it a natural candidate for the smallest useful chunk boundary.
3. Detecting Sentence Boundaries
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446842509-230550292.png
Splitting on a period sounds simple, but abbreviations and decimals both use periods too.
A naive splitter breaks sentences in the wrong places without care.

blocks.text: 4. Single Sentence Chunks Versus Groups
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446842510-332929750.png
One sentence per chunk maximizes precision; grouping a few sentences preserves more surrounding context.
The same tradeoff of chunk size and context from Why Chunking reappears here.
5. Losing Cross Sentence Context
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446842511-977297494.png
A single, isolated sentence can lose the context that only the surrounding sentences would have supplied.
A pronoun or reference in that sentence may point to something outside the chunk entirely.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A sentence like "It grew rapidly after that" means nothing on its own once isolated as a chunk. Whatever "it" refers to lives entirely in a neighboring sentence that got left out.

blocks.text: 6. Sentence Chunking And Embedding Quality
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446842511-218197775.png
The same retrieval precision benefit from Why Chunking applies here: a short, focused sentence embeds very precisely.
That trades surrounding context for maximum topical focus.
7. Handling Very Short Sentences
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446842512-727824505.png
A very short sentence carries little standalone meaning on its own.
Merging it with a neighboring sentence often produces a more useful chunk.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A one or two word sentence like "Not always." provides almost no retrievable signal by itself, so most sentence chunking implementations merge such fragments with an adjacent sentence.

blocks.text: 8. Sentence Chunking Relative To Other Strategies
Sentence chunking is essentially recursive chunking's finest possible granularity.
In the ordered list of separators from Recursive Chunking, the sentence level is simply the last structural fallback before word breaks.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Sentence Chunking Is The Right Granularity

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Sentence Chunking Is The Right Granularity
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446842512-240100943.png
Precise fact lookup and short answer retrieval suits sentence chunking well.
Content needing broader surrounding context needs larger chunks or overlap instead, covered in this module.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates splitting text into sentences and merging short fragments.

code.content:
import re

document = (
    "Dr. Smith joined the company in 2020. "
    "She led the research team. "
    "Yes. "
    "Her work focused on retrieval systems."
)

def split_sentences(text):
    # detecting sentence boundaries
    # a naive splitter would wrongly break after "Dr." here
    protected = text.replace("Dr.", "Dr<PERIOD>")
    raw_sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", protected)
    return [s.replace("Dr<PERIOD>", "Dr.").strip() for s in raw_sentences if s.strip()]

def merge_short_sentences(sentences, min_length=10):
    # handling very short sentences
    merged = []
    for sentence in sentences:
        if merged and len(sentence) < min_length:
            merged[-1] = merged[-1] + " " + sentence
        else:
            merged.append(sentence)
    return merged

sentences = split_sentences(document)
print("Raw sentences (detecting sentence boundaries):")
for s in sentences:
    print(f" {s!r}")

merged = merge_short_sentences(sentences)
print("\nAfter merging short fragments:")
for s in merged:
    print(f" {s!r}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows "Dr. Smith" staying intact instead of being wrongly split after the abbreviation, and the standalone "Yes." fragment merged into its neighboring sentence.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Splitting naively on every period, breaking abbreviations and decimal numbers incorrectly.
Leaving very short, low information sentences as standalone chunks instead of merging them.
Using single sentence chunks for content where cross sentence context matters.
Never comparing single sentence chunks against small sentence groups to see which retrieves better.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Sentence chunking treats each individual sentence, or a small group of them, as its own chunk.
A sentence already expresses one complete idea, making it a natural chunk boundary candidate.
Detecting true sentence boundaries is harder than splitting on every period, due to abbreviations.
Single sentence chunks maximize precision; grouping sentences preserves more surrounding context.
An isolated sentence can lose context that only its neighbors would have supplied.
Short, focused sentences embed very precisely, trading context for topical focus.
Very short sentences carry little standalone meaning and are often merged with a neighbor.
Sentence chunking is essentially recursive chunking pushed to its finest granularity.
